records.name: Lesser Poland Voivodeship
records.summary:
Małopolska adopted a voivodeship-level "LGBT-ideology-free" resolution in 2020, repealed on 20 September 2021 under EU funding pressure, placing it in the same five-region configuration as the eastern belt. The regional declaration carried the same intent as its siblings: to exclude a visible public LGBTQ presence from the voivodeship's civic space.

Within the same unit, however, Kraków—the capital and Poland's second city—has moved decisively the other direction. In May 2024 newly elected mayor Aleksander Miszalski announced he would become the first Kraków mayor ever to attend the city's LGBT Equality March and would fly a rainbow flag at city hall. His predecessor Jacek Majchrowski (2002–2024) had only become an honorary patron of the march in 2021 and never attended. For a visitor in Kraków's old town, the operative institutional signal is the mayor's public presence, not the repealed voivodeship document.

sources.summary: The Them (23 September 2021, updated 29 September): Małopolska's voivodeship council repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution on Monday 20 September 2021 alongside Podkarpackie and Lubelskie, after European Commission funding threats — Małopolska notable because council leader Jan Duda (father of president Andrzej Duda) had only weeks earlier voted to keep the zone. Confirms the record's 2020-21 voivodeship arc and its EU-pressure repeal date.

Notes from Poland (9 May 2024): newly elected Kraków mayor Aleksander Miszalski announced in one of his first decisions that he would attend the city's annual LGBT Equality March — becoming the first Kraków mayor to do so, after a predecessor who declined — and pledged to hang a rainbow flag at city hall, writing that he wants 'a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone'. Dated local-government signal of warming climate in the voivodeship's capital.

records.name: Łódź Voivodeship
records.summary:
Łódzkie was one of the five voivodeships that formally adopted an "anti-LGBT ideology" resolution by mid-2020, placing approximately one-third of Poland's territory under declarations whose stated purpose was to exclude LGBTQ public events. It sits in the PiS-vote heartland belt running east of the Łódź metro area. The resolution was struck down or repealed in the 2021 wave following EU Commission funding threats.

No march ban, coordinated attack, or county-level holdout comparable to Subcarpathian's Łańcut (2025) or Podlaskie's Białystok County is documented for Łódzkie. The sub-national finding is the regional resolution itself and its location in the eastern conservative bloc; the practical visitor-facing exposure is the general social climate of that bloc rather than a specific enforcement or violence event.

sources.summary: Per-voivodeship revocation record: the Supreme Administrative Court of Poland revoked Łódź Voivodeship's anti-LGBT resolution on 12 October 2023, and the Świętokrzyskie voivodeship council revoked its own resolution on 22 September 2021 (the European Commission had written to the governors of five voivodeships — Lublin, Łódź, Lesser Poland, Podkarpackie, and Świętokrzyskie — on 2 June 2020 about the resolutions). By 24 April 2025 all anti-LGBTQ resolutions and all Local Government Family Rights Charters in Poland had been withdrawn or invalidated by court order.

Between 2019 and 2025 more than 100 Polish local governments adopted ‘LGBT-free zone’-style resolutions which at their peak covered roughly a third of the country's land area; Polish administrative courts struck them down as unconstitutional (Article 32 equal treatment), the European Commission linked EU development funds to their repeal, and the last remaining zone (in Łańcut) was abolished in 2025. The article notes the resolutions were symbolic and institutional rather than criminal — they created no new penalties and barred no one physically — but signalled to local bureaucracies and schools which families and identities local leadership considered legitimate.
